prompt: Which of these classes answers a GET in milliseconds, with no restore first?
hint: One archive class has "instant" in its name.

choices.text: Glacier Deep Archive
choices.why: Deep Archive has to be restored first, and a restore takes up to 48 hours.

choices.text: Glacier Flexible Retrieval, when read with the Expedited tier
choices.why: Expedited is a restore that takes 1 to 5 minutes; the GET only works after it.

choices.text: Glacier Instant Retrieval
choices.why: Right. It is priced like an archive and read like Standard, with a fee per GB read.

choices.text: None of the Glacier classes; only Standard
choices.why: Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval are both read in milliseconds.

prompt: An object of 100 GB is written to Glacier Deep Archive (0.00320 USD per GB-month, 180 days minimum) and deleted after 30 days. Counting a month as 30 days, how many USD of storage is it billed in all?
hint: It is billed for the minimum, not for the days it stayed.

prompt: Quitanda keeps the only copy of its signed supplier contracts. Why is One Zone-IA the wrong class for them, even though they are rarely read?

choices.text: It keeps the data in one zone, so losing that zone loses the contracts
choices.why: Right. One Zone-IA fits data that can be produced again, never the only copy.

choices.text: It is slower to read than Standard-IA
choices.why: Both are read in milliseconds; the difference is where the copies live.

choices.text: It refuses objects smaller than 128 KB
choices.why: It accepts them and bills them as 128 KB, like Standard-IA.

choices.text: It has a minimum duration of 180 days, which a contract kept for years would exceed anyway
choices.why: Its minimum is 30 days; 180 is Deep Archive's. And a long minimum would not matter for data kept for years.

prompt: Match each class to its minimum storage duration.
hint: Three classes share a minimum with another.

prompt: A program reads `StorageClass` from `head-object` and finds no such field in the answer. What class is the object in?
hint: Compare the two `head-object` answers in the section.

choices.text: None yet: the class is assigned when the object is first read
choices.why: Every object has a class from the moment it is written.

choices.text: Standard
choices.why: Right. `head-object` leaves the field out for Standard, and a program has to read the absence that way.

choices.text: The bucket's default class, which `get-bucket-location` reports
choices.why: There is no default class per bucket; the class is per object, and the call named reports a region.

choices.text: Intelligent-Tiering, whose tier changes and so is not printed
choices.why: An Intelligent-Tiering object prints `"INTELLIGENT_TIERING"`, as the section on it shows.

prompt: In the API and in `--storage-class`, the archive class whose fastest restore takes 1 to 5 minutes is written `___`.
hint: It kept its name when the product was renamed.

prompt: Quitanda copies 2,000 objects onto themselves to move them from Standard-IA to Glacier Instant Retrieval, ten days after writing them. What does the copy cost beyond the new class's price?
hint: Each copy is a request, and the old objects leave early.

choices.text: Nothing: a change of class is free and keeps the old object's age
choices.why: The copy writes a new object; the `LastModified` moved in the section.

choices.text: A restore fee for every object, since Glacier classes are written by restore
choices.why: A restore is for reading an archived object, and Instant Retrieval has none.

choices.text: 90 days of Glacier Instant Retrieval, charged at once
choices.why: The minimum is charged only if the object leaves early; nothing is charged in advance.

choices.text: 2,000 COPY requests, and the remaining 20 days of Standard-IA for each object
choices.why: Right. A copy is priced like a PUT, and the objects left Standard-IA inside its 30-day minimum.

prompt: In moto, `head-object` right after a Bulk restore from Deep Archive shows `ongoing-request="false"`. What would S3 show at that moment?
hint: How long does a Bulk restore from Deep Archive take?

choices.text: The same, because S3 restores small objects at once
choices.why: The documented times do not depend on size; the restore is a job in a queue.

choices.text: No `Restore` field, until the restore has been approved by the account's owner
choices.why: There is no approval step; the field appears with the request.

choices.text: `ongoing-request="true"`, for up to 48 hours
choices.why: Right. Every GET would keep failing with `InvalidObjectState` until it finished.

choices.text: An error, because a Bulk restore cannot be asked of Deep Archive
choices.why: Bulk is one of Deep Archive's two tiers; Expedited is the one it does not have.

prompt: A restore job tested only against moto asks Deep Archive for the Expedited tier, and every test passes. What happens on AWS?
hint: Look at the tiers the documentation lists for Deep Archive.

choices.text: S3 refuses the request: Deep Archive has only Standard and Bulk
choices.why: Right. moto accepted a tier S3 does not offer, which is the lesson's point about a moto success.

choices.text: It works and is ready in 1 to 5 minutes, at the Expedited price
choices.why: Those are the Expedited times for Glacier Flexible Retrieval, not for Deep Archive.

choices.text: S3 quietly downgrades it to Bulk
choices.why: S3 does not change a tier for you; an invalid one is an error.

choices.text: It works, since moto and S3 accept the same tiers
choices.why: moto checks less than S3; its acceptance is not evidence of S3's.

prompt: After a restore from Deep Archive finishes, what does `StorageClass` say for the object?
hint: The restore makes a temporary copy.

choices.text: `STANDARD`, until the days asked for run out
choices.why: The object stays in its class; the readable copy is temporary and has no class of its own here.

choices.text: `DEEP_ARCHIVE`
choices.why: Right. To move it for good, restore it and then copy it onto itself in another class.

choices.text: `GLACIER`, because the command line calls both archive classes that
choices.why: The warning of `aws s3 cp` does; the API reports the real class, `DEEP_ARCHIVE`.

choices.text: `RESTORED`
choices.why: There is no such class; the state of a restore is in the `Restore` field.

prompt: What happens to a 40 KB object written with `--storage-class INTELLIGENT_TIERING`?
hint: There is a size below which the class does not watch.

choices.text: It is refused, being under the 128 KB minimum
choices.why: It is accepted; the 128 KB line decides whether it is monitored, not whether it is stored.

choices.text: It is billed as 128 KB, like in Standard-IA
choices.why: That rule belongs to the IA classes and Glacier Instant Retrieval.

choices.text: It stays in the frequent tier at Standard's price and pays no monitoring fee
choices.why: Right. It is never moved, so the class gives it nothing and charges it nothing extra.

choices.text: It moves to the infrequent tier after 30 days without a read
choices.why: Only monitored objects move, and objects under 128 KB are not monitored.

prompt: Quitanda has 4 million objects of 1 MB each in Intelligent-Tiering. At 0.00250 USD per 1,000 objects a month, what is the monitoring fee for one month, in USD?
hint: The fee is per object, whatever its size.

prompt: In moto, `put-bucket-intelligent-tiering-configuration` failed with `IllegalLocationConstraintException`. What is the right reading?
hint: What is that error normally about?

choices.text: moto does not implement the call, and the request reached the code that creates buckets
choices.why: Right. It says nothing about Intelligent-Tiering on AWS, which this part of the lesson teaches from the documentation.

choices.text: The bucket must be in us-east-1 to use the archive tiers
choices.why: The error names a location, and that is a symptom of the routing; the archive tiers are available in São Paulo.

choices.text: The configuration has a syntax error
choices.why: A malformed argument is refused by the command line with `ParamValidation` before anything is sent.

choices.text: The archive tiers need versioning on the bucket
choices.why: They do not, and the error would name versioning if they did.

prompt: Using the table, after how many full reads a year does a terabyte in Glacier Instant Retrieval cost more than the same terabyte in Standard?
hint: 101.99 for the year, 30.72 per full read, against 497.66.

choices.why: At four reads the reads cost more than its own storage, 122.88 against 101.99, and the total is still far below Standard.
That is Standard-IA's break-even with Standard, at 10.24 a read.

choices.text: It never does: an archive class is always cheaper
choices.why: Its reads are the dearest in the table, so enough of them overtake Standard.

prompt: Why does `year.py` print a dash, not 0.00, for One Zone-IA's read?

choices.text: One Zone-IA charges nothing to read
choices.why: Then it would print 0.00, like Standard.

choices.text: One Zone-IA objects cannot be read back
choices.why: They are read in milliseconds, like Standard-IA.

choices.text: Python cannot multiply by a price below 0.02
choices.why: It multiplies Deep Archive's 0.00320 in the next row.

choices.text: The sheet prints no retrieval price for it, and an unknown price is not zero
choices.why: Right. `None` is a price the sheet does not have, and printing it as zero would be a guess dressed as a number.

prompt: A dataset of 1 TB is read in full every week. Which class does the arithmetic of the section put it in?
hint: Count 52 reads and compare with the break-evens.

choices.text: Standard-IA, the class for data that is read
choices.why: 52 reads at 10.24 add 532.48 to 271.56, far above Standard's 497.66.

choices.text: Glacier Instant Retrieval, because it is read in milliseconds
choices.why: Read in milliseconds, yes, at 30.72 a read: 52 of them are 1,597.44.

choices.text: Standard
choices.why: Right. Standard-IA breaks even at about 22 full reads a year, and 52 is far past it.

choices.text: Deep Archive at bulk speed, the cheapest total in the table
choices.why: The table's total is for one read; a weekly read could not wait 48 hours.

prompt: Match each kind of Quitanda data to the class that fits it.
hint: Ask how often it is read and how soon it is needed.

pairs.left: Today's orders, read by every report
Order photos read only when a customer disputes a delivery, months later
Audit exports kept seven years, requested with weeks of notice
Thumbnails that can be made again from the originals

prompt: Order the classes by the price of keeping a GB for a month, cheapest first.
hint: Deep Archive is the floor and Standard the ceiling.

prompt: Quitanda wants to archive 50 million click events of 2 KB each, one object per event. Which of these are real costs of that plan on AWS? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think per object, not per gigabyte.

choices.text: In Glacier Instant Retrieval, each event is billed as 128 KB
choices.why: Yes: 64 times its size.

choices.text: In Deep Archive, each event carries 40 KB more than its own bytes
choices.why: Yes: 32 KB at the archive price and 8 KB at Standard's.

choices.text: 50 million PUT requests to write them
choices.why: Yes: one request per object written, whatever the class.

choices.text: In Intelligent-Tiering, a monitoring fee on each event
choices.why: Objects under 128 KB are not monitored and pay no fee; they stay at Standard's price.
